text:
The rain poured relentlessly over the quiet coastal town of Shorehaven, casting an eerie gloom over its cobblestone streets. Detective Eleanor Briggs tightened her coat against the chill as she arrived at the grand but crumbling Rosewood Manor. Inside, the body of Victor Langston, a reclusive millionaire and former art dealer, lay sprawled in front of the enormous fireplace, his once-pristine maroon robe now stained with blood. Standing in the room were four individuals, each with a story to tell: Celia Langston, Victor’s ambitious and much younger wife; Jonas Mercer, his quiet and brooding nephew; Dr. Margaret Hensley, a family friend and trusted physician; and Grant Walker, Victor’s loyal but secretive estate manager. Detective Briggs studied their faces— grief, shock, and something more elusive— as the sound of thunder rolled across the darkened skies.

###

Detective Briggs began her inquiry with Celia, who sat stiffly in an armchair, her eyes red but strangely dry. “I was in my room reading when I heard the crash,” Celia said, her voice trembling just enough to sound convincing. “When I came down, Victor was already… like that.” Briggs noted the diamond bracelet on Celia’s slender wrist, glinting in the flickering firelight—a stark contrast to the gloom of the room. It was no secret that Victor and Celia’s marriage had been fraught; whispers around town hinted at frequent arguments over Victor’s iron grip on his vast fortune. Still, Celia’s performance seemed practiced, as if she had rehearsed her reaction. “Victor was difficult, yes,” she added, her voice dropping, “but I loved him. I didn’t always agree with how he treated people, but I would never hurt him.” 브iggs felt the first threads of doubt crawl into her mind.

###

Jonas Mercer, the lanky and brooding nephew, stood leaning against the wall as if trying to disappear into the shadows. He flicked his cigarette nervously, the faint scent of smoke mixing with the smell of damp wood and old books. "Uncle Victor wasn’t exactly a saint," Jonas muttered when Briggs turned her gaze to him. "Do you know how many people hated him? Half the town, maybe more. I’m sure some of them are celebrating right now." Briggs raised an eyebrow. "And where were you tonight, Mr. Mercer?" Jonas hesitated, his eyes darting toward the broken clock above the fireplace. "Out for a walk by the cliffs," he finally said, his voice defensive. "I needed—space." Briggs noted the muddy remains on his boots, the kind one would get from Shorehaven’s notorious cliffside paths, and the corner of her mouth twitched. "Convenient time for a solitary stroll," she remarked, and Jonas scowled, retreating further into the shadows. Something about his discomfort felt genuine—perhaps too genuine. 

###

Dr. Margaret Hensley, poised and composed despite the tension in the room, adjusted the glasses perched on her sharp nose as Detective Briggs shifted her attention to her. “Victor had his flaws,” she admitted coolly, her voice steady, “but he was my patient and my friend. I was here tonight because he asked me to come by—he’s been complaining of chest pains for weeks.” Margaret glanced briefly at Victor’s lifeless body, her expression unreadable. “I left him in the study after our conversation. He seemed unusually anxious, but I assumed it was about his health. I went to the kitchen to make tea and was there when I heard the commotion.” Briggs studied Margaret for a long moment, noting the subtle way she gripped the strap of her handbag, knuckles tight. “Did Victor mention anything specific that might have caused his anxiety?” Briggs asked. Margaret hesitated, the faintest crack appearing in her veneer. “Not in detail, no,” she finally said. “But he did mention trouble with… trust.”

###

Grant Walker, the estate manager, stood apart from the others, his burly frame tense as he stared out the rain-streaked window. His finely pressed suit was immaculate, save for a dark smudge near the cuff of his left sleeve that Briggs couldn’t help but notice. When asked to account for his whereabouts, Grant turned, his deep voice measured and calm. “I was in the storage room cataloging inventory for the manor. Mrs. Langston can confirm—she called for me earlier in the evening to help with some glassware she wanted packed away.” His eyes flicked briefly to Celia, an unreadable look passing between them, before he added, “After that, I returned to the storage room until I heard the shouting.” Briggs tilted her head, her sharp gaze unwavering. “Shouting?” she repeated. Grant nodded tightly. “That’s when I came running. By the time I arrived, it was too late.” His tone was somber, but there was a guardedness in his demeanor, as though he was carefully calculating each word he chose to say—or not say.

###

As Detective Briggs moved around the room, her eyes combing over the details, she couldn’t ignore the shattered crystal decanter lying near Victor’s body. A thin trail of dark liquid—whiskey, perhaps—had soaked into the ornate rug. “Did anyone touch this?” she asked, her finger pointing at the shards. Celia shook her head, her voice faint. “It was already broken when I came in.” Jonas snorted from his corner. “Victor loved that decanter. You couldn’t breathe near it without him losing his temper.” Margaret chimed in, her voice laden with calm authority. “He was drinking from it earlier. He mentioned needing ‘something strong to think.’” Briggs crouched down, carefully picking up a larger shard. It was sharp, its edges jagged but clean. A possible weapon—or a reckless accident? Her gaze shifted to Grant, whose smudged sleeve suddenly stood out in harsher relief. He opened his mouth to speak but then snapped it shut, his jaw tightening. Something about his composed exterior seemed to waver under the mounting scrutiny. "Interesting," Briggs murmured to herself, tucking the shard into her evidence bag.

###

Detective Briggs moved to the fireplace, inspecting the ash-streaked mantel where Victor’s blood had sprayed. Alongside the scattered items of everyday use—a brass clock, a porcelain figurine—was a single muddy footprint on the stone hearth. It was faint but unmistakable. “Someone stepped here,” Briggs said aloud, drawing the group’s attention. Her eyes flicked to Jonas’s boots, still caked with dirt from the cliffs. Jonas stiffened under her scrutiny. “What? You think I’d kill my own uncle and then tromp my filthy boots across the crime scene?” he snapped, his defensive tone bolstering the suspicion in the air. “It’s not like I’m the only one who’s been outside tonight,” he added pointedly, glaring toward Grant, who stood quietly with his arms crossed, his expression unreadable. Briggs frowned, her keen mind turning over the facts as the group’s energy shifted uneasily. Someone had tried hard to conceal their movements—but the evidence had clearly spoken otherwise.

###

Briggs turned her attention back to Jonas, her eyes narrowing. “You said you were walking near the cliffs—but that doesn’t explain how mud from outside ended up inside, on the hearth of all places.” Jonas glared at her, his jaw tightening, but before he could respond, Celia cut in, her voice sharp. “Jonas had plenty of reason to despise Victor. He was jealous of him, always complaining that Victor treated him like a charity case. Isn't that right, Jonas?” Her accusation hung heavy in the room as Jonas’ face flushed with frustration. “Oh, give me a break, Celia,” he shot back, his voice rising. “You’re not exactly innocent here. Everyone in this house knows you’ve been scheming to get your hands on Uncle Victor’s money from day one.” Celia’s mouth fell open in mock outrage, but her hand instinctively went to the diamond bracelet again, a subtle and telling movement. Briggs observed the exchange carefully, noting how quickly Jonas had deflected—and how conveniently the smear on Grant’s sleeve lingered unaddressed in the silence that followed.

###

Detective Briggs decided to break the tension by shifting her line of questioning. She walked over to the side table near Victor’s body, where an empty glass rested next to an open book. The glass had a reddish-brown residue clinging to its bottom, faint but visible under the dim light. She held it up. “This doesn’t look like whiskey.” Margaret stepped forward, her tone measured. “Victor had a habit of drinking herbal remedies in the evenings. I often prescribed them to help with his nerves.” Briggs raised an eyebrow. “Strange. If that’s the case, why does the smell suggest something stronger?” Margaret hesitated, her composure slipping ever so slightly. “It’s possible he mixed it with alcohol tonight. He wasn’t always… consistent with my advice.” Jonas let out a soft laugh, bitter and cold. “Or maybe someone else decided what went in his drink. Isn’t that right, Margaret? Always at his beck and call, always ‘prescribing’ things for him. What exactly was in the glass tonight?” Margaret turned sharply toward him, her eyes flashing. “How dare you insinuate anything,” she snapped. But the flicker of unease in her expression wasn’t lost on Briggs.

###

Briggs set the glass down carefully and stood, folding her arms as she regarded Margaret. “You seem awfully defensive, Doctor. It’s a reasonable question—what exactly did you give Victor tonight?” Margaret squared her shoulders, regaining a fraction of her composure. “Chamomile and valerian root,” she replied evenly. “Nothing harmful, Detective. You can test the residue if you like.” Before Briggs could press further, Grant’s voice cut through the room, low and steady. “Doesn’t it strike anyone as odd that Jonas is so quick to point fingers? He seems very interested in steering suspicion away from himself.” All eyes turned to Jonas, who gave a hard, humorless laugh. “Oh, sure, blame the guy who’s been the family scapegoat since he could walk. Typical.” But his deflection didn’t go unnoticed by Briggs, who took a step closer to the fireplace once more. She crouched down near Victor’s body, her sharp eyes locking onto the faint smear near one of the bloodstains—the outline of a shoeprint. “Jonas,” she said slowly, tilting her head toward the sole of his boot, “do you mind showing me something?” Jonas froze, his posture stiffening as the room fell silent.

###

Jonas hesitated for a moment too long, his eyes darting from Briggs to the others in the room. Finally, with a huff, he stepped forward and lifted his foot slightly, revealing the pattern on the sole of his boot. Briggs knelt down, comparing it to the faint shoeprint near the fireplace. It was muddy, smeared, but the pattern—small ridges and grooves—was strikingly similar. “Care to explain this, Mr. Mercer?” Briggs asked, her tone calm but unwavering. Jonas shoved his hands in his pockets and glared at her. “I… I don’t know,” he muttered. “Maybe I stepped there earlier. I’ve been in this room before tonight, you know.” “Before or after Victor was killed?” Briggs pressed. Before Jonas could respond, Celia’s voice rang out, sharp and accusatory. “Why don’t you just admit it already? You’ve always resented him! You probably lost your temper again, didn’t you?” Jonas turned on her, his voice rising. “Don’t you dare try to pin this on me, Celia! If anyone had a reason to want Victor dead, it’s you!” The room erupted into layered accusations, but Briggs’s mind stayed focused, piecing together the threads of truth tangled in the chaos.

###

“Enough!” Briggs barked, her commanding tone slicing through the cacophony of voices. Silence fell as all eyes turned to her. She straightened up from the fireplace and leveled the group with a piercing gaze. “Let’s stop playing games. Someone in this room knows exactly what happened to Victor, and no amount of mud on boots or shouting will cover that up.” Her words lingered like the lingering scent of smoke in the air. With deliberate steps, she approached the desk in the corner of the room. On its surface, amidst scattered papers and an antique fountain pen, lay a sheet of paper partially crumpled, its edges smeared with faint gray fingerprints. Briggs picked it up carefully and scanned it. 

It was a hastily written note, in Victor's unmistakably shaky handwriting: "No longer trust. It ends tonight." Victor’s strained final thoughts spoke volumes, but they also raised questions. "‘No longer trust,’" Briggs murmured aloud, her eyes briefly flicking from Celia to Jonas, then to Grant and Margaret. “What exactly was about to ‘end tonight?’” Margaret cleared her throat, her voice quieter than before. “Victor was paranoid. Lately, he suspected… betrayal. Financial matters, mostly. He thought someone was stealing from him.” At this, Celia visibly flinched, her hand still resting on the glittering diamond bracelet. But it was Jonas, standing stiffly at the edge of the room, who spoke next, his voice heavy with apprehension. “If you think this note proves something, you should ask yourself who stood to gain the most from him being gone.” His eyes flicked directly to Celia, the implication unmistakable.

###

Celia’s face paled, but she quickly composed herself, her sharp features tightening into a mask of indignation. She raised her chin, her voice laced with venom. “That’s rich coming from you, Jonas. You’ve been leeching off Victor for years, always complaining about how the inheritance wasn’t being handed to you on a silver platter. You had just as much to gain—if not more—than I did.” Jonas took a step forward, his fists clenched at his sides. “Oh, please. Don’t pretend you didn’t marry him for the money. Everyone knows it. You’ve been waiting for Victor to die since the moment you said ‘I do.’” 

“Enough!” Briggs interjected, her voice sharp, cutting through the tension as she moved toward the desk again. Her fingers hovered over the note for a moment before pulling open one of the desk drawers. Inside were scattered documents, notes, and a small velvet pouch. She lifted the pouch and carefully opened it, spilling its contents into her palm—shimmering rubies, small but dazzling. “These don’t look like they belong with the rest of Victor’s financial concerns,” Briggs remarked coolly. “Anyone care to explain them?” Margaret stepped forward, her face grim. “Victor bought those recently,” she said. “He planned to have them set into a necklace for Celia. He said… he wanted to make up for how he’d neglected her.” 

Celia’s lips pressed into a thin line, but her hand instinctually moved toward the bracelet again—this time with hesitation. “He never mentioned it to me,” she muttered. Briggs’s focus darted between Celia and the rubies. “Interesting,” the detective murmured. “Because I suspect Victor’s paranoia wasn’t just about stolen money—it was about trust being fractured from within this house.”

###

Briggs returned the rubies to the pouch and placed it in her pocket for now, her sharp gaze lingering on Celia. “Trust is a funny thing, isn’t it?” she said evenly, her words hanging in the thick air. “For someone with so much at stake, Victor seemed increasingly unsure of the people closest to him. Tell me, Celia—why do you think Victor never gave you the necklace? Cold feet? Or maybe he realized something was off.” Celia’s expression hardened, but before she could answer, Grant cleared his throat from his spot by the window.

“If Victor had trust issues, they weren’t misplaced,” Grant said, his deep voice cutting through the palpable tension. He straightened, his eyes narrowing as he looked at Margaret. “Why don’t you tell the detective about the ‘arrangements’ you and Victor discussed in private? Seems to me you were always whispering to him about what should be signed over to whom.” 

Margaret’s posture stiffened, her sharp features darkening with irritation. “What are you implying, Mr. Walker? That I had something to gain? Please. Victor trusted me because I was one of the few people who actually cared about his well-being,” she snapped. Her gaze darted toward Briggs, her composure faltering just slightly. “I wasn’t stealing from him, if that’s what he told you, Detective. He was a very sick man—physically and emotionally. He was paranoid, and he often misread people’s intentions.”

Briggs watched this exchange closely, her mind turning over the competing accusations. “And where does that leave you, Mr. Walker?” she asked, turning to Grant. “You’ve been conspicuously quiet about what Victor may or may not have suspected of you." Grant bristled, his jaw tightening as his eyes flicked to the stained cuff of his sleeve. “I’ve been his loyal employee for years. If he didn’t trust me, he never said as much.” But the discomfort in his tone betrayed him, and Briggs felt her instincts tugging her toward something deeper beneath the surface.

###

Briggs stepped closer to Grant, her gaze bearing down on him. “Loyal employees don’t usually turn up with smudges on their clothing that they can’t explain,” she said, pointing to the dark stain on his cuff. Grant opened his mouth to respond, but his words faltered, a flicker of unease crossing his otherwise stoic face. “It’s nothing,” he muttered, looking away. “A mark from the storage crates. I told you, I was in the storage room before this happened.”

Briggs tilted her head, unconvinced. “And yet the mud on your sleeve suggests something different. Mud that doesn’t come from inside the house but from outside—just like the mud on Jonas’s boots. Maybe you’d like to revise your statement, Mr. Walker?” Grant’s lips pressed into a firm line, but before he could answer, Jonas let out a sharp laugh. “Oh, look at that—finally, someone else is in the hot seat. I guess the ‘loyal estate manager’ routine doesn’t hold up under pressure, does it, Grant?”

Grant turned on Jonas, his composure cracking just enough for his voice to rise. “Why don’t you keep your mouth shut, you spoiled little leech? Everyone knows you’ve been angling for Victor’s money and nothing else. You have no idea what loyalty even means!” The room bristled with tension as their words bounced off the walls, each accusation tearing further through the brittle veneer of civility. Briggs observed silently, watching with clinical precision as the fractures in everyone’s stories grew deeper. Slowly, she reached into her pocket and pulled out the broken shard from the crystal decanter, holding it up for the group to see. “I wonder,” she said, her voice even yet firm, “if loyalty or betrayal matters much when blood ends up spilled all the same.” Her words cast a shadow over the argument, and once again, silence thickened the air as Briggs turned her attention, waiting for someone to slip.

###

The silence grew heavy as Briggs turned the shard of crystal over in her hand, the flicker of firelight catching on its jagged edges. “This decanter—shattered, yet still here in the room, inches from Victor’s body,” she began. Her eyes moved deliberately from one face to the next. “If this was the weapon used to strike Victor, it’s curious how no one seems to recall hearing it break. A crash like that would echo, wouldn’t it?”

Celia shifted in her chair, crossing her arms tightly over her chest. “It must have broken when—when he fell,” she stammered, though her voice wavered, as if the excuse didn’t even convince herself. Briggs tilted her head but said nothing, letting the silence stretch until Celia dropped her gaze to the floor.

Grant, standing stiffly by the window, clenched his jaw and added, “Maybe someone cleaned it up in a hurry. Or maybe they came in here after the fact, trying to make it look like an accident.”

“And who do you think this mysterious ‘someone’ is?” Briggs asked, her tone sharp as she expertly baited him. Grant hesitated, his jaw working under unspoken stress, before his eyes flicked toward Jonas. “I wouldn’t put it past him,” he muttered. “He’s got the temper for it.”

Jonas raised his hands mockingly, his voice dripping with sarcasm. “Ah, yes, blame the angry nephew. How original, Grant. Tell me, are you going to explain that mud on your sleeve to us, or are you too busy throwing me under the bus?”

Briggs stepped between them, holding up the shard like a warning. "Let’s not get too carried away with accusations." She pointedly examined both Grant and Jonas. “The mud is troubling, yes, but so is the absence of sound. If no one heard the decanter break, then there are two possibilities: Someone’s lying about where they were at the time, or this decanter didn’t break during Victor’s fall—it broke before.” Her gaze snapped to Margaret now, whose sharp intake of breath didn’t go unnoticed. “Tell me, Doctor, you seem awfully silent all of a sudden. Anything you’d like to add about Victor’s final moments?” 

###

Margaret folded her arms tightly, her face pale but her voice resolute. “I already told you everything I know, Detective. By the time I came back from the kitchen, it was too late. I didn’t hear the decanter break because I wasn’t in the room.” Her tone was defensive, but there was a subtle waiver in it—just enough for Briggs to catch.  

“You returned to the kitchen to make tea,” Briggs said, repeating Margaret's earlier statement with deliberate slowness. “How long were you gone, exactly? Minutes? Longer?” Margaret hesitated, her hands tightening around the strap of her bag as the others in the room watched her intently. “Five minutes, maybe less. Victor was alive when I left him,” she answered curtly.  

Celia, sensing the spotlight shifting from her, seized the moment. “But you were the last person to see him alive, weren’t you, Margaret? And didn’t you often bring him drinks? Who’s to say you didn’t give him something… extra tonight?” Her voice dripped with insinuation, and while she didn’t hide her disdain for Margaret, it was clear she was also trying to save her own neck.  

Margaret snapped back, her voice sharp. “How dare you? I’m a doctor, not a murderer. Whatever Victor consumed, he poured himself—I saw him drinking alone in this room before I left.” But her words opened another door in Briggs’s mind. If Victor had indeed been drinking alone, whose fingerprints, other than his, would possibly be on the broken decanter? And if Margaret was telling the truth about his paranoia, perhaps he’d poured himself a drink to steady his nerves… only for that drink to betray him.  

Briggs’s eyes flicked to the stained glass on the side table and then to Jonas, whose agitated pacing had started again. Her instincts told her there was more here—carefully planted crumbs of evidence pointing in several directions at once. “Victor trusted you, Margaret," Briggs said softly, deliberately. "But trust has its limits, doesn’t it? Especially when what’s left behind doesn’t match the picture we're being shown.”

###

Margaret’s face paled further, but before she could respond, Jonas’s pacing suddenly stopped, and his voice rang out with sudden force, cutting through the tense atmosphere. “Is anyone going to acknowledge the obvious here?” he said, his tone bitter. “Victor didn’t trust any of us, but he trusted her the least,” he spat, pointing directly at Celia. “This whole circus about tea and decanters? It all comes down to her. She’d been fighting with Victor for months—months! And don’t think we didn’t hear it, Celia. I heard you screaming at him in this very room just last week about changing his will!”

Celia bolted upright from her chair, her face twisting in outrage, though there was a flicker of fear in her eyes. “What are you talking about? That was nothing but a—a heated discussion. He was trying to cut me out, and I was defending myself. A normal reaction for a woman whose husband refuses to trust her!” She looked frantically toward Briggs, trying to sound convincing. “If I wanted Victor dead, why would I have fought him to stay in his will?” 

“Maybe,” Jonas sneered, “because you knew damn well you wouldn’t get a dime otherwise. You were desperate, Celia. And that bracelet?” He pointed to the glittering diamonds on her wrist. “Victor gave you everything you wanted. And as soon as he hesitated, as soon as the gravy train slowed down, you couldn’t take it anymore.” 

“Enough,” Briggs said sharply, though her mind couldn’t ignore the fire in Jonas’s accusation. From what she’d learned, Victor’s will had been a contentious subject for everyone in the room. “You’re saying Celia had motive because of the will. But motive alone isn’t proof.” 

Jonas leaned back against the wall, his expression dark. “Fine. But if anyone here had a motive strong enough to kill Victor, it was her. And don’t tell me you haven’t noticed.” His voice trailed off as his eyes settled on the fragments of glass near the body—the broken decanter. Detective Briggs noted how everyone followed his gaze, their tension thickening further. Jonas had placed Celia in the spotlight again, but something about his determination to shift attention left Briggs uneasy. She wasn’t done unraveling how deep his own involvement might go.

###

As the uneasy silence stretched out, Detective Briggs moved deliberately toward the fragmented decanter, crouching beside Victor's body once more. She ran her gloved fingers lightly over the shards scattered on the rug, her sharp eyes catching a small chip of glass stained with blood. Straightening up, she held it aloft, her gaze falling squarely on Celia. “Jonas makes a good point about your fights with Victor,” Briggs said evenly. “His accusations aside, I can’t help but wonder about your reaction tonight—calm, but just a little too practiced. Tell me, Mrs. Langston, why were you so quick to accuse others, even before I started asking the hard questions?”

Celia opened her mouth to respond, but Grant stepped in, his voice cutting across hers. “Because she’s hiding something, that’s why.” His jawline was tight, his eyes locked on her like a predator ready to pounce. “Victor might not have trusted the rest of us, but with her, it was worse. The fights weren’t about the will—that’s what she wants everyone to think. It was about her sneaking around, whispering with lawyers, trying to leave him before he could leave her penniless.”

“That’s not true!” Celia snapped, finally finding her voice, though her cheeks visibly reddened. Her hand trembled as she instinctively clutched the bracelet again, a stark gesture that Briggs couldn’t ignore. “Victor... Victor was controlling, paranoid, impossible to reason with! I had no reason to kill him—I just wanted him to trust me again!”

“And yet,” Briggs said, cutting through Celia’s frantic defense, “here we are, with Victor dead and all four of you pointing fingers in all directions. If this really comes down to trust, how about we follow the evidence instead of the noise?” She held the bloodied shard higher, letting the group focus on it. “A shard like this could deliver a fatal blow, and it’s consistent with the injuries Victor sustained. But here’s what’s curious—it would’ve taken force to break this decanter, force that feels a lot more deliberate than a drunken accident.”

Briggs's words hung heavy in the air, laced with insistence. Her keen eyes swept the room, probing for the subtle cracks in every facade. “So, I’ll ask again—who here had the nerve to shatter trust, so violently and permanently, in this very room?"

###

The room fell deathly silent, the only sound coming from the rain hammering against the large windows. Celia glanced at the shard in Briggs’s hand, her lips trembling as though she wanted to speak, but no words came. Jonas leaned against the fireplace, his dark eyes blazing with frustration, while Grant folded his arms tightly, glaring at everyone but saying nothing. Margaret, standing nearest to the door, finally broke the silence with a low, steady voice. “If you want the real culprit,” she said, her tone cold and deliberate, “you should ask yourself who would risk everything by staying in this house tonight... instead of running.”

All eyes turned sharply to her, but Briggs tilted her head, unfazed by the implication. “An interesting theory, Doctor. Staying often speaks of guilt, but then again, so does hiding in plain sight.” Her voice dropped slightly, her words directed at everyone but landing on Jonas deliberately. “Tell me, Mr. Mercer, you were quick to throw Celia under the bus. Quite a considerable effort for someone who claims to have nothing to hide.”

Jonas straightened, his already rigid posture stiffening further. “What the hell does that mean?” he barked. “I’ve been trying to help you figure out who did this! But it seems easier for you to target me just because of some stupid muddy boots.”

“Stupid boots, no,” Briggs challenged, her gaze sharp. “But I can’t help noticing how you keep narrating your way out of suspicion—advising me where to look, conveniently focusing my attention on everyone else. Deflection is a classic strategy. And, Jonas, frankly, you’re not subtle.” She placed the shard of glass into a separate evidence bag, her tone now ice-cold. “Let’s talk about anger. From everything I’ve gathered tonight, it seems you had the most volatile relationship with Victor. He resented how you squandered opportunities, didn’t he? He once cut you off financially before softening again. But perhaps tonight… he made it clear this time was permanent.”

Jonas’s mouth opened, but no words came. Grant’s lip curled into a faint sneer. “That’s a damn good theory, detective. Except I seem to remember someone else’s shirt sleeve being more interesting than my nephew.” He glanced smugly at Briggs, but she didn’t take the bait, her eyes still firmly pinned on Jonas.

###

Jonas clenched his fists, his face darkening as the weight of Briggs’s words settled over the room. “You think I killed him because we fought? Because he cut me off?” His voice cracked slightly, revealing a fragile edge. “Yeah, we argued. A lot. But I didn’t have to kill him to get back at him. He treated me like I was nothing, and that wasn’t going to change whether he was alive or dead.”  

Briggs raised an eyebrow, stepping closer to him. “Yet you were out on the cliffs tonight—alone. You come back with mud on your boots, and we have a shoeprint on the hearth that matches. I’d say that’s more than just an unlucky coincidence.”  

Jonas shook his head vehemently. “I didn’t go near him! And what about Grant?” He jabbed a finger toward the estate manager, his voice rising with desperation. “How come no one’s questioning why his sleeve is stained? Or why he always seemed to know where Victor kept everything valuable? Who says he didn’t snap when Victor found out?”  

Grant glared at Jonas, his voice tight with irritation. “I’ve explained myself. I wasn’t anywhere near Victor when this happened, and the stain is from the work I was doing earlier. You’re grasping at straws, Mercer.”  

“Am I?” Jonas growled, taking a step toward Grant. “You’ve been his watchdog for years, always keeping tabs on who he did and didn’t trust. Maybe tonight Victor finally realized you were the one keeping secrets, so you silenced him.”  

“That’s enough,” Briggs interrupted, her voice firm and commanding. “It’s convenient for all of you to turn on each other, but this mess wasn’t created by trust alone—it was created by manipulation. And one of you here has been spinning the threads just long enough to tie up the rest in knots.” She turned her back on them for a moment, pacing toward the bookshelf to collect her thoughts. Then, in a calm but deliberate voice, she said, “Victor might not have trusted you, Jonas. But you were desperate. Maybe not for his approval, but for the life you’d lose without his support.” She turned back, her eyes narrowing. “And desperation is a dangerous thing.”

###

Jonas’s face turned crimson, his jaw tightening as Briggs’s words pinned him further into the corner. “You don’t know a damn thing about me,” he snapped, the anger in his voice barely concealing the tremor underneath. “Victor didn’t just cut me off financially—he humiliated me. He loved to remind me I was dependent on him while he controlled everything. But that doesn’t mean I killed him!”  

“And yet,” Briggs said coolly, taking a measured step closer to Jonas, “you were the only one who had both the motive and the opportunity. The muddy boots, the suspicious print on the hearth… what were you doing near the fireplace tonight, Jonas? Because from where I’m standing, it looks like you were right here when everything unfolded.”

Before Jonas could respond, Celia suddenly spoke up, her voice sharp as a blade. “Why are you still focusing on him when the real danger is standing right there?” She pointed at Grant, her confidence returning as her voice grew louder. "Victor barely trusted Jonas, but he *relied* on Grant. That stain isn’t as innocent as he claims. And let’s not forget who knew where in this house Victor liked to keep his most valuable—”  

“You’re desperate, Celia,” Grant interrupted, his voice an irritated growl. “Anything to keep the attention off yourself. We all know you weren’t exactly the grieving wife.”  

Briggs ignored their squabble, her attention rooted on Jonas. “Desperation,” she repeated softly, her voice slicing through the accusations flying across the room. “That’s the key word, isn’t it, Jonas? You’ve been wearing it on your face all night. Something brought you to that fireplace. You said Victor treated you like you were nothing, that he humiliated you. What happened tonight? Did he finally say something you couldn’t forgive?”

Jonas’s eyes flashed angrily as the room fell quiet again, but instead of answering, he took a single step back, his shoulders squaring defensively. His silence only deepened the suspicion hanging over him, and Briggs wasn’t about to let it slip away unnoticed. “You know what happened,” she pressed. “You’ve been deflecting because you’re too afraid to admit it—but it’s all starting to unravel now. Care to tell me the truth, or should I piece together the rest?”

###

Jonas looked at her, his face pale but his eyes flashing with defiance. “Fine,” he spat, his voice raw with emotion. “You want the truth? Yes, I was at the fireplace. I came in after Victor had been drinking, after he’d started ranting about being betrayed—by me, by everyone. He kept saying he was changing the will, that he was done with me for good. So, yes, I argued with him!” His voice rose, trembling with frustration. “We shouted, and I lost my temper. But I didn’t touch him! He was fine when I left the room! Someone else went in after me.” His eyes darted toward Celia and then Grant, his words taking on the tone of a desperate man defending himself. “I swear, when I walked out, he was alive... angry, but alive.”

Briggs’s gaze didn’t waver as she studied him. “You argued, you walked out… and yet you left behind a print near the body. Why step up on the hearth unless you were close enough to…” She let the question hang in the air, but Jonas cut her off.  

“I don’t know! Maybe I was too close. Maybe I… maybe I stepped there by instinct during the argument. I wasn’t thinking! But that doesn’t prove I killed him!” he shouted, his voice cracking again.  

Margaret, who had been standing silently in the corner, stepped forward suddenly, her voice sharp. “Victor didn’t need any of you to kill him. You’re all missing the point. Victor was paranoid, unstable—he kept talking about poisoning himself ‘to escape the betrayal.’ I warned him not to overindulge... but none of you listened. The drink, the broken glass... Are we even sure someone here killed him?” 

A murmur of shock rippled through the room, but Briggs simply shook her head, her calm demeanor slicing through the noise. “No, Margaret,” Briggs said slowly. “Victor didn’t poison himself. He was struck—deliberately, with force. This wasn’t an escape. This was personal. And what I can’t help but notice is how everyone in this room keeps pointing fingers at each other… as if hoping it’ll keep me from seeing the truth.” Her eyes swept the group, sharp and calculating.

###

The air in the room felt thick as Briggs paced slowly, her eyes darting between each suspect. "You," she began, pointing briefly toward Celia, who flinched, "are desperate to pin this on anyone but yourself. A tumultuous marriage, a motive wrapped in money, and yet… you didn’t have the nerve. Your panic tonight isn’t guilt—it’s fear of losing everything now that Victor's gone." Celia’s sharp intake of breath was the only sound she made, her trembling hands still clutching the bracelet.

Briggs turned her attention to Grant next. “And you, Mr. Walker. The loyal estate manager with a suspicious stain on his sleeve. I’ll admit, it made me wonder for a time. Maybe Victor caught on to something you were doing behind his back. But the truth is, you’re too careful. Too calculating. That stain might implicate you in something sloppy, but not murder.” Grant’s shoulders relaxed slightly, but his glare at Jonas remained sharp.

Briggs stopped and faced Margaret, whose calm mask now seemed dangerously close to cracking. “Margaret,” she said softly, “the trusted family friend. The doctor who knew every detail of Victor’s health, and who conveniently claims to have been making tea during the exact window he was killed. You had the perfect opportunity to strike when no one would suspect you. And yet,” Briggs paused, her voice dropping, “you left behind no forensic evidence. No proof you were anywhere near the body in that critical moment.”

She turned abruptly, her piercing gaze landing squarely on Jonas. “But you, Jonas. The angry nephew. The one with muddy boots, a shoeprint by the hearth, and years of resentment churning beneath the surface. You’ve done everything in your power to throw the suspicion onto Celia, Grant, even Margaret. But in doing so, you’ve unraveled your own story. The mud on your boots wasn’t from your cliffside walk—it was from this room, when you stepped too close in the midst of your argument. You shattered the decanter against your uncle in a fit of rage and didn’t have time to clean your tracks.”

Jonas stepped back, his face drained of color. “That’s not… I didn’t…!” But his voice faltered, the weight of the evidence pressing down on him. Briggs continued, relentless. “Victor’s paranoia worsened, didn’t it? He accused you of betrayal. He threatened to cut you off for good. And you lost control.” She gestured toward the broken glass near the fireplace. “That print, the shattered decanter—it all points back to you. Care to explain again what happened, Jonas?” Silence followed, but his trembling hands told Briggs all she needed to know.

###

Jonas’s trembling hands curled into fists, his knuckles whitening as the weight of Briggs’s words bore down on him. His lips parted, but the defiance in his eyes had vanished, replaced by something raw and bare—fear and regret. “It wasn’t supposed to happen like this,” he muttered, his voice barely audible at first, then rising as the dam of his restraint finally broke. “He pushed me too far! He called me a failure, a waste of his charity! I just—” His voice cracked, and he looked around the room as though searching for someone who might absolve him. “I just wanted him to stop.”

Briggs remained silent, her sharp gaze steady as the others watched in stunned silence. Jonas staggered back a step, the truth spilling from his lips now in a torrent. “We were by the fireplace arguing—you’re right, I lost it. I grabbed the decanter; I just wanted him to listen, to stop talking to me like I was nothing. But he grabbed my arm, and it... it broke. I didn’t mean to—” His voice choked as his guilt overwhelmed him. “But when I saw the blood, I panicked. I left before anyone came in. I didn’t know what to do.” He slumped against the wall, his head in his hands. “I—I didn’t mean to kill him.”

Celia let out a sharp, stunned gasp, and Margaret pressed a hand to her mouth, her carefully composed mask shattered. Grant’s expression darkened, his jaw tight, but he said nothing, only shaking his head at the raw confession. Briggs straightened, her voice calm but firm as she addressed him. “Intent matters, Jonas. You lost control, and Victor paid for it with his life.” She turned to the uniformed officers waiting just outside the door. “Take Mr. Mercer into custody.”

As the officers moved toward Jonas, he offered no resistance, the fight drained out of him. Celia turned away, unable to look at him, while Margaret stared at the floor, her usual sharpness dulled by shock. Grant stood by the window, his expression unreadable, the rain falling outside marking the end of a long, harrowing night.

Detective Briggs watched as Jonas was led away, the weight of the confession leaving the room eerily quiet. The tangled web of betrayal and mistrust had finally unraveled, but Briggs knew this was more than just another case; it was a grim reminder that the deepest wounds often came from those closest to the heart. She glanced back at the now-empty fireplace, the faint scent of whiskey and regret lingering in the air, and then stepped out into the rain, letting the storm cleanse the darkness of the night.
